create_chat_completion.title: Generate a chat completion
create_chat_completion.description:
The main inference call. Send a list of messages and get the model's reply.
`deployment_id` is the name of a DEPLOYMENT on this resource, not a model name -- see the pack notes. A 404 with `DeploymentNotFound` means the name is wrong, not that the model does not exist.
`messages` is the usual shape: `[{"role": "system", "content": "..."}, {"role": "user", "content": "..."}]`. Pass `tools` to let the model call functions, and `response_format` of `{"type": "json_object"}` to force valid JSON -- which only works if the prompt also asks for JSON.
Streaming is not supported here, so a long completion takes as long as it takes and arrives in one piece. Check `choices[0].finish_reason`: `stop` is a complete answer, `length` means max_tokens cut it off, and `content_filter` means Azure blocked it.
create_chat_completion.notes: deployment_id is a deployment name, not a model name. Streaming is not supported.

deployment_id.description: The deployment name on this Azure OpenAI resource -- what someone chose when deploying the model, not the model's own name.

messages.description: The conversation, each {"role": "system"|"user"|"assistant"|"tool", "content": "..."}. A system message first sets the behaviour.

max_tokens.description: Cap on the tokens generated. A completion that stops with finish_reason "length" hit this.

temperature.description: Randomness, 0 to 2. Around 0 for extraction and classification, 0.7 for open-ended writing. Adjust this or top_p, not both.

top_p.description: Nucleus sampling threshold, 0 to 1. An alternative to temperature.

stop.description: Up to four strings that end generation when produced.

frequency_penalty.description: Penalise tokens by how often they have appeared, -2 to 2.

presence_penalty.description: Penalise tokens that have appeared at all, -2 to 2.

seed.description: Ask for repeatable sampling. Best-effort, not a guarantee.

tools.description: Function definitions the model may call, each {"type": "function", "function": {"name": ..., "parameters": ...}}.

tool_choice.description: none forbids tool calls, auto lets the model decide, required forces one.

response_format.description: Set to {"type": "json_object"} to force syntactically valid JSON. The prompt must also ask for JSON, or the model may produce an endless run of whitespace.

user.description: A stable end-user identifier, for abuse monitoring.

output.description: The completion, with usage and content-filter results.

choices.description: Each with message (role, content, tool_calls), finish_reason and content_filter_results.

usage.description: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens and total_tokens -- what the call cost.

prompt_filter_results.description: How Azure's content filter graded the prompt.

model.description: The model the deployment actually served.

create_completion.title: Generate a text completion (legacy)
create_completion.description:
The older prompt-in, text-out endpoint, for deployments of legacy completion models such as gpt-35-turbo-instruct. Chat models are not reachable this way -- use create_chat_completion for those, which is what almost everything should use.
Kept for deployments that predate the chat format.
create_completion.notes: Only works for deployments of legacy completion models. Chat models need create_chat_completion.

deployment_id.description: The deployment name of a legacy completion model.

stop.description: Up to four strings that end generation.

n.description: How many completions to generate. Each is billed.

user.description: A stable end-user identifier, for abuse monitoring.

choices.description: Each with text, index, finish_reason and content_filter_results.

create_embeddings.title: Turn text into embedding vectors
create_embeddings.description:
Produce embedding vectors for one or more pieces of text, for semantic search, clustering or a vector index.
`deployment_id` must be a deployment of an embedding model -- text-embedding-3-small, -3-large or ada-002. Pointing it at a chat deployment returns an error.
Batch: `input` takes a list, and embedding many strings in one call is far cheaper in round trips than one at a time. The vectors come back in `data`, in the same order as the input.
Every vector in an index must come from the SAME model -- dimensions differ between models, and even where they match the spaces are not comparable. Mixing them produces confident nonsense.
create_embeddings.notes: All vectors in one index must come from the same embedding model. Dimensions and spaces are not interchangeable.

deployment_id.description: The deployment name of an embedding model.

input_texts.description: The texts to embed. Batch as many as fit rather than calling once per string.

dimensions.description: Shorten the vectors to this many dimensions. Supported by the text-embedding-3 models only, and the index must be built at the same size.

user.description: A stable end-user identifier, for abuse monitoring.

output.description: One vector per input, in the same order.

data.description: Each with index and embedding, the float vector.

model.description: The embedding model the deployment served.

create_image.title: Generate an image from a prompt
create_image.description:
Generate images with a DALL-E deployment. Returns URLs by default -- which expire after about an hour, so download anything worth keeping promptly -- or base64 with `response_format` of `b64_json`.
Azure rewrites prompts for safety and returns the rewritten version as `revised_prompt` on each result. That is the prompt that was actually used, and it is worth reading when the output is not what you asked for.
A prompt the content filter rejects returns 400 with a `ResponsibleAIPolicyViolation` code rather than an image.
create_image.notes: Returned URLs expire after about an hour. Prompts are rewritten for safety; check revised_prompt.

deployment_id.description: The deployment name of a DALL-E model.

prompt.description: What to draw. Up to 4000 characters.
prompt.example: A watercolour of a lighthouse in a storm

n.description: How many images to generate. DALL-E 3 supports only 1.

size.description: Image dimensions. The non-square sizes cost more.

quality.description: hd produces finer detail and costs more than standard.

style.description: vivid is dramatic and hyper-real; natural is more restrained.

response_format.description: url returns expiring links; b64_json returns the image inline.

user.description: A stable end-user identifier, for abuse monitoring.

data.description: Each with url or b64_json, revised_prompt and content_filter_results.

list_models.title: List the models available on this resource
list_models.description:
Every model this Azure OpenAI resource can serve, with its capabilities, lifecycle status and deprecation dates. `capabilities` says whether a model supports chat completion, embeddings, fine-tuning and inference, which is how you find out whether a model can do what you want before deploying it.
This is not the list of DEPLOYMENTS. A model appearing here can be deployed; whether it currently is, and under what name, is the resource's own configuration.
list_models.notes: Lists deployable models, not the deployments that exist. Inference needs a deployment name.

output.description: The models the resource can serve.

items.description: id, status, capabilities (chat_completion, embeddings, fine_tune, inference), lifecycle_status and deprecation.

create_batch_job.title: Submit a batch of requests for offline processing
create_batch_job.description:
Run a large set of chat or embedding requests offline at roughly half the cost of calling them one at a time. The trade-off is latency: a batch has a 24-hour completion window and may take most of it.
`input_file_id` is a file already uploaded to the resource containing one JSON request per line -- upload it with another client, since this API takes multipart form data that this connector cannot send, then find its id with list_files.
Poll get_batch_job until `status` is `completed`, then read `output_file_id` with get_file_content.
create_batch_job.notes: Requests are processed within 24 hours, not immediately. The input file must be uploaded by another client.

input_file_id.description: Id of an uploaded JSONL file with one request per line, from list_files.

endpoint.description: Which API the batched requests target.

completion_window.description: How long the service has to finish. Only 24h is supported.

metadata.description: Arbitrary key-value metadata to attach to the job.

id.description: The batch id; poll get_batch_job with it.

list_batch_jobs.title: List batch jobs
list_batch_jobs.description: The batch jobs on this resource, newest first, each with its status and request counts. `status` moves through validating, in_progress, finalizing and completed -- or failed, expired or cancelled.

after.description: Continue after this batch id, for paging.

items.description: id, status, input_file_id, output_file_id, error_file_id, request_counts and created_at.

get_batch_job.title: Get a batch job's status
get_batch_job.description:
Follow a batch job. `request_counts` shows total, completed and failed, which is how you tell partial success from total failure -- a batch reaching `completed` with failures still produces an `error_file_id` alongside the output.
Once `status` is `completed`, read `output_file_id` with get_file_content for the results and `error_file_id` for the requests that did not work.

batch_id.description: The batch id, from create_batch_job or list_batch_jobs.

output.description: The batch job and its progress.

status.description: validating, in_progress, finalizing, completed, failed, expired or cancelled.

output_file_id.description: File holding the results, once completed.

error_file_id.description: File holding the requests that failed.

cancel_batch_job.title: Cancel a batch job
cancel_batch_job.description: Stop a batch that is still validating or in progress. Requests already completed stay completed and are still billed, and their results remain available in the output file -- cancelling stops further work rather than undoing what has been done.
cancel_batch_job.notes: Requests already processed are still billed and their results are kept.

list_files.title: List files uploaded to the resource
list_files.description:
The files stored on this Azure OpenAI resource -- batch inputs and outputs, fine-tuning training sets, and the error files jobs produce. Each has an id, a purpose and a size.
Uploading is not possible through this connector (it needs multipart form data), so this is how you find the id of a file another client uploaded.

purpose.description: Only files with this purpose -- fine-tune, batch, batch_output, assistants.

items.description: id, filename, bytes, purpose, status and created_at.

get_file_content.title: Download a file's contents
get_file_content.description:
Read a stored file. This is how batch results come back: the `output_file_id` from a completed batch job holds one JSON response per line, matching the requests in the input file by their `custom_id`.
Also how to read an `error_file_id` and find out which requests failed and why. The content is returned as text.

file_id.description: The file id, from list_files or a batch job's output_file_id.

delete_file.title: Delete a file
delete_file.description: Remove a stored file. Irreversible. A file still referenced by a running batch or fine-tuning job should be left alone until the job finishes -- deleting a batch's output file loses the results permanently, since they are not stored anywhere else.
delete_file.notes: Deleting a batch's output file destroys the only copy of the results.

list_fine_tuning_jobs.title: List fine-tuning jobs
list_fine_tuning_jobs.description: Fine-tuning jobs on this resource, each with its status, base model and -- once finished -- the `fine_tuned_model` name. That name still has to be DEPLOYED before it can be used for inference; a completed fine-tune is not yet callable.
list_fine_tuning_jobs.notes: A completed fine-tuned model must be deployed before create_chat_completion can use it.

after.description: Continue after this job id, for paging.

items.description: id, status, model, fine_tuned_model, training_file, hyperparameters and created_at.

create_fine_tuning_job.title: Start a fine-tuning job
create_fine_tuning_job.description:
Fine-tune a base model on a JSONL training file already uploaded to the resource. Training takes hours and is billed by token, so this is not a call to make casually.
`training_file` is a file id from list_files whose purpose is `fine-tune`. A `validation_file` is strongly worth supplying: without one there is no honest way to tell whether the model learned or memorised.
Leave `hyperparameters` alone unless you have a reason -- the defaults Azure picks from the dataset size are usually better than a guess. Poll get_fine_tuning_job for progress.
create_fine_tuning_job.notes: Training takes hours and is billed by token. The resulting model still needs deploying before use.

model.description: The base model to fine-tune, e.g. gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18.

training_file.description: File id of the JSONL training set, from list_files.

validation_file.description: File id of a held-out validation set. Strongly recommended -- without it you cannot tell learning from memorisation.

suffix.description: A suffix for the resulting model name, up to 40 characters.

hyperparameters.description: n_epochs, batch_size and learning_rate_multiplier. The defaults Azure derives from the dataset are usually better than a guess.

id.description: The job id; poll get_fine_tuning_job with it.

status.description: pending or running at this point.

get_fine_tuning_job.title: Get a fine-tuning job's status
get_fine_tuning_job.description:
Follow a fine-tuning job. `status` moves through pending, running and succeeded, or fails. On success `fine_tuned_model` names the new model -- which then has to be deployed on the resource before create_chat_completion can call it, since inference addresses deployments rather than models.
`trained_tokens` is what the run cost.

output.description: The fine-tuning job and its progress.

status.description: pending, running, succeeded, failed or cancelled.

fine_tuned_model.description: The resulting model name, on success. Must be deployed before use.

trained_tokens.description: Tokens processed, which is what the run was billed on.

cancel_fine_tuning_job.title: Cancel a fine-tuning job
cancel_fine_tuning_job.description: Stop a fine-tuning job that is pending or running. Tokens already processed are still billed, and no usable model comes out of a cancelled run -- so cancelling is a way to stop spending, not a way to get a partial result.
cancel_fine_tuning_job.notes: Tokens already processed are billed, and the run produces no usable model.

list_fine_tuning_events.title: Get a fine-tuning job's progress log
list_fine_tuning_events.description: The event log of a fine-tuning run -- per-epoch training loss, validation loss where a validation file was given, and any warnings. This is where you find out whether the model is actually improving or has started overfitting, which the job's `status` alone never tells you.

after.description: Continue after this event id, for paging.

items.description: id, created_at, level, message and data holding step, train_loss and valid_loss.
